title: Would you book the extra shift?

beats.say: In this example our regular shift can take one specialist case in five. Turn over the first five messages. One needs a specialist. Put that share on the ruler. Twenty percent, right on the staffing line. If you had to pencil in a shift now, which would you book?

Keep those five on the rail. Open the rest of the first hundred. Watch the pink cases accumulate. Sixteen need a specialist. Out of a hundred, that's sixteen percent. Now the dot sits below the same staffing line. Draw the interval for these hundred reviews. It still reaches past the staffing line.

Before opening any messages, we drew four hundred distinct IDs at random from this week's hundred thousand. This tray is the first of those four stacks. We also fixed the staffing rule in advance. We'll decide after all four hundred reviews.
If the whole interval for the week's rate falls below twenty percent, keep the regular shift. Otherwise, book the extra shift. Let's see how far a sample estimate can move.

title: Watch a counted batch become one point

beats.say: For this simulation, set the underlying rate to sixteen percent. Each message independently gets one of two labels. Counting the specialist labels gives a binomial count. Count one random batch of a hundred. Its fraction becomes this point. Repeat with fresh independent labels. Each point is one complete sample, while the rate stays fixed.

Pick the furthest point from the middle. Its hundred messages came from the same sixteen-percent world as every other point. Change which messages you draw, and the estimate moves. That spread is sampling variation.

Give each sample four hundred labels. Watch the second cloud form on the same scale. Four times the independent labels roughly halves the standard error, the typical movement of the estimate. Extra labels buy precision gradually.

title: Keep the candidate rates that pass

beats.say: Our tray still has sixteen specialist cases. Multiply the sample share by the routine share, divide by a hundred, then take the square root. This estimated standard error is just under four percentage points. The quick Wald interval extends one point nine six standard errors on each side of sixteen percent. Its width comes from the labels in this tray.
Slide a candidate population rate across the axis. At twenty percent we'd expect twenty cases, with a standard deviation of four. We saw sixteen. That's one standard deviation away.

For a two-sided ninety-five percent Wilson interval, keep the candidates that put our count within one point nine six standard deviations of the expected count. Include both endpoints. Each candidate supplies its own scale. Where does the curve cross the cutoff?

Project the two crossings down. The accepted rates run from about ten to twenty-four percent. That is the Wilson interval. It crosses our twenty-percent staffing threshold, so this sample supports rates on either side. We still have three hundred planned reviews to finish.

title: What changes when more labels arrive?

beats.say: Set the weekly audit aside. Build a tray on purpose with four pink marks among twenty-five labels. The yellow dot marks our sample estimate. Imagine adding another tray with exactly the same mix. What will happen to the dot? What will happen to the ends of the interval?

Slide in the second tray. Eight pink marks out of fifty put the dot right back where it was. Bring in the remaining trays. Watch the caps draw closer with every group of twenty-five. The gray whisker shows where they started.

At four hundred labels the sample estimate is still sixteen percent. Look halfway between the caps on each whisker. The Wilson midpoint moved closer to the yellow dot. We gave every tray the same mix to isolate the effect of sample size. In a real draw, the sample estimate can move too.

title: Which population rates fit the labels?

beats.say: Open ten messages. All ten stayed with the regular team. Which population rates could plausibly have given us that tray?

Wald uses a zero estimated standard error and collapses there. Wilson still accepts rates above zero. With zero positives, the upper end of a two-sided ninety-five percent Wilson interval has a shortcut. One point nine six squared is about three point eight four. Keep the square in the calculation so we round only the final answer.

Divide that square by the number of independent labels plus the same square. Put ten in the denominator. Work out the fraction on the screen. The upper endpoint is about twenty-seven point eight percent.
Open ten more independent messages. These are all routine too. You have twenty reviewed, zero positives. Keep the numerator. What goes in the denominator now, and how high can the interval reach?

Put twenty where ten used to be. Keep the same square in both places and divide. The upper end comes down to sixteen point one percent. A population rate anywhere from zero up to about that value is still compatible with twenty clean labels under this model.
Go back to ten. Now suppose all ten messages need a specialist. Flip the interval across the scale. Rates from about seventy-two percent to one hundred percent fit these ten labels.

The last interval used ten messages. Each simulated interval uses a fresh sample of one hundred. Fix the population rate at sixteen percent. Draw twenty-four independent samples and give each its own Wilson interval. Watch for a whisker that misses the fixed line.

Two miss in this run. Ninety-five percent describes the method's approximate coverage across repeated samples. Actual coverage depends on the rate and sample size. To predict the fraction in a future sample, you'd also have to account for the variation in those new labels.

title: Which messages did the sample leave out?

beats.say: This separate queue has a thousand messages. Seven hundred are routine. The rest concern billing or account access. Select only routine questions, drawing a hundred messages at random without replacement. More routine labels tighten this example's interval around the same twelve percent. The blue whisker uses a binomial approximation.

Here we've drawn four hundred of just seven hundred eligible cases. A finite-population correction would reduce the standard error. Even reviewing every routine case would tell us nothing about the other two lanes' rates.

Suppose we also know the specialist rate in each lane. Twelve percent of seven hundred routine questions contribute eighty-four expected specialist cases. At twenty-five percent of two hundred, billing adds fifty. At forty-two percent of a hundred, account access adds forty-two.
Join those contributions and divide by all thousand messages. The whole queue's rate is seventeen point six percent.

In a real queue those lane rates need evidence. Sample across the target queue. Every message can enter the same draw. Follow ten message IDs into one tray. Or draw a random sample within each lane. Take three messages apiece for this example. Each tray now estimates its own lane's rate. Weight each lane's estimated rate by its share of the target traffic. Routine supplies seventy percent of the queue, billing twenty, and account access ten. Carry uncertainty from each sample into the weighted result.

title: Reuse the labels, retain their identities

beats.say: Back to our original hundred reviewed messages. Bootstrap draws reuse those IDs with replacement. Press the first selected message onto the strip. Its source stays put. The second draw picks the same pink message. Look at the two imprints. Finish all hundred draws. Count their specialist marks and compute one fraction.

Add that fraction to the histogram. Repeat the whole draw, count, and deposit. Each completed resample adds one entry. Their spread approximates sampling movement using our observed labels as the stand-in population. Take the two and a half and ninety-seven and a half percentiles for a percentile interval. Extra repetitions refine the calculation while the original evidence stays at a hundred labels.

Suppose the tray contains ten zeros. Make a thousand resamples of ten, drawing with replacement. Every resample is all zeros. The percentile interval collapses. Where would a positive have come from? There is another trap when several rows arrived together. Keep that group together when the sampling design depends on it.

title: What do the labels tell us about the rate?

beats.say: Here are those first five messages again. One specialist case in five gives us twenty percent. Under the binomial model, that's the rate that makes this count most likely. It's our maximum-likelihood estimate. Now suppose we start with a Beta two-two prior.

It gives rates near one half more weight before we see any labels. To find the peak after seeing these five, add one success term and one failure term. The peak moves to two sevenths, about twenty-nine percent.
We call that posterior peak the maximum a posteriori estimate, or MAP. For this prior, add one to the positive count and two to the total count. Those prior terms come from our starting assumptions.

Bring back the full hundred labels. Sixteen needed a specialist, so the blue mark goes at sixteen percent. Keep the same two prior terms. The posterior peaks at seventeen over a hundred and two, about sixteen point seven percent. Compare the two rows.
With five labels the prior moved the estimate almost nine percentage points. With a hundred it moves the estimate less than one point.

Now compare a held-out forecast. This is a separate audit of messages kept out of training. Choose one score bucket before looking at outcomes. Every message in it got a twenty-percent chance of needing a specialist. Draw one hundred held-out messages at random from that bucket.
Suppose sixteen need a specialist. Is that four-point gap enough to call the forecast wrong?

Place the Wilson interval for the bucket's outcome rate across the forecast line. Twenty percent still fits. The observed gap could come from sampling variation. A larger random audit of this bucket could resolve a smaller gap. We'd need held-out labels from the other score buckets to assess those forecasts too.

title: Keep the denominator attached to the target

beats.say: Point to the whole queue. That is our population. Its unknown specialist share is the estimand. To estimate it, draw messages at random and review every one you drew. Divide the specialist count by the number reviewed. That rule is our estimator.

Today's sixteen percent is one estimate. Transfer the question to flagged signups. Only flagged signups reach the tray. The fraction of those flags that are abusive estimates review precision. Recall needs all abusive signups in the denominator. The false-positive rate needs all clean signups. Prevalence needs the full signup stream.

A different audit drew a hundred messages. Sixteen pink cases went to a specialist. Sixty-four blue ones stayed with the team. Twenty envelopes are still sealed. If you want the rate among the cases we've actually resolved, where would you close the bracket?

Count the eighty open cases. Sixteen out of eighty is twenty percent. That answers the question about the cases the reviewers have finished. Widen the bracket to the whole tray. Suppose none of the sealed cases needs a specialist. Sixteen out of a hundred is sixteen percent.

Suppose all twenty need one. Thirty-six out of a hundred is thirty-six percent. Those bounds describe this tray. To estimate the rate in the queue, we also have to allow for which hundred messages our random draw picked.

If difficult cases take longer to resolve, dropping them can systematically shift our answer. Report how many we selected, how many we resolved and how many are still waiting. Look at this one. The customer got back in, then the account locked again.
Does that need a specialist? Freeze the labeling rule and hide the model score. Give two reviewers the same case. Each records a label in private.

Now compare their labels. One chose routine. The other chose specialist. Record that disagreement. Put their answers beside three more cases they both reviewed in private. Read across each row. On how many cases did they agree?

Three pairs match. Divide by all four double-reviewed cases. That's seventy-five percent observed agreement in this little set. Save both original labels. Now send the disputed case for adjudication. The final label can go into the audit, and we'll still know how often the reviewers agreed on their own.

This audit selected whole campaigns at random, then reviewed every signup inside them. Pull one signup from the pink campaign. Now pull its neighbor. They came in on the same draw. In this example all the signups in a campaign have the same outcome.
Count the groups on the left. How many independent draws gave us these hundred labels?

Ten campaigns. Two were positive and eight were negative. Try drawing whole campaigns again, with replacement. Here's the same campaign twice. Each copy brings all ten of its signups. We could instead put the hundred rows in a bowl and draw them one at a time.
Which method will give a wider spread of sample fractions?

Draw rows one at a time. The two and a half and ninety-seven and a half percentiles are twelve and twenty-eight percent. Now draw whole campaigns. Those percentiles reach from zero to fifty percent. Each pink draw moves ten labels together.
The variance is the success rate times the failure rate, divided by the number of independent draws. Using a hundred in place of ten makes that variance ten times too small.

This redraw has twenty abusive signups out of a hundred. Look at the last campaign. If you changed one signup from clean to abusive, the abusive count would reach twenty-one. Could a whole-campaign redraw give us that count? Swap one negative campaign for a positive one. All ten signups change together. Thirty abusive signups out of a hundred. With only ten independent campaigns, those coarse steps limit how closely a percentile interval can track its target coverage.
If campaigns differ in size, keep each signup count with its campaign when you redraw. A campaign of twenty brings twice as many labels as a campaign of ten. These two draws bring thirty signups.

title: Where does the gap come from?

beats.say: Go back to our three lanes. Imagine a population with the same mix and rates. Make ten thousand independent draws from the routine lane, sampling with replacement. Individual estimates vary from audit to audit. Their expected average stays at twelve percent. Follow the gap to the whole population's rate.

Billing and access never had a chance to get into any tray. That's why the average estimate stays five point six percentage points low even as the scatter shrinks. That persistent gap is the estimator's bias. Mean squared error adds its square to the sampling variance.

A prior moves the estimate for a different reason. With a Beta two-two prior, one success in five gives a Beta three-six posterior. Its mode, the peak of the green curve, is two sevenths. Its mean lies a little farther right, at three ninths. For this prior, the posterior mean adds two to the positive count and four to the total count.
Both use the same five observed labels. Say which summary you used and name the prior. Wilson's adjusted midpoint comes from a score test.

For calibration, we set aside outcomes from one score bucket. The interval around its observed rate includes the forecast. The other buckets are still empty. Choose your bins before inspecting outcomes. If you search many bins for a gap, account for those multiple comparisons.

For sampling variation, draw more representative labels. For an ambiguous case, check the labeling rule and independent agreement. If a new type of traffic arrives, collect evidence from it. You may hear irreducible ambiguity called aleatoric uncertainty and lack of knowledge called epistemic uncertainty.

title: Which denominator goes with each claim?

beats.say: Here is another tray. Nine pink, thirty-six blue, fifteen still sealed. What fraction of the resolved cases went to a specialist? Among all sixty, what's the lowest fraction that could need one? What's the highest?

Close the bracket around the reviewed cases. Nine out of forty-five is twenty percent. We can make that claim while the last row is still sealed. Now include all sixty. Suppose the fifteen envelopes are all routine. Nine out of sixty is fifteen percent.

Suppose every sealed case needs a specialist. Twenty-four out of sixty is forty percent. Those are the limits of what could already be in our tray. A confidence interval for the queue answers a different question.

title: Make the decision, then uncover the week

beats.say: The first hundred reviews gave us the gray interval. It crosses the staffing line. The three unopened stacks belong to the same random draw. Review the remaining three hundred IDs. That completes our planned sample.

Four hundred out of a hundred thousand is small enough for the binomial approximation here. Across all four hundred, sixty-four need a specialist. The dot is still at sixteen percent. Look at the magnified scale. The pink mark is the regular team's limit.
Which side of the pink line must the upper cap land on for us to keep the regular shift?

The cap stops at nineteen point nine one percent. That is just below twenty percent. Under the rule we set before review, we choose regular staffing. Save the count and its interval with the schedule.
Include how the team drew the messages and reviewed them independently. How much of that capacity did the team actually use?

Eighteen thousand of its hundred thousand messages went to a specialist. Fill the regular team's capacity with those cases. Two thousand places stayed open. In sampling and simulation, we'll choose a model for the incoming messages and draw whole weeks from it. How often would the team need that extra shift?
